Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 8

The Handshake
at Lexington

Stone’s Christians and Campbell’s Disciples · 1831–1835
Chapter 8. Last week: the Millennial Harbinger, a movement living toward God’s future. This morning: can they unite with anyone, even each other?
Where we are

The story so far

1801  Cane Ridge: thousands at one table
Ireland  Thomas Campbell works for union among divided Seceders, in a violent, war-torn land
1807  In America, he serves the Supper to Presbyterians of other sects, and is tried for it
1808–09  Alexander, shipwrecked in Scotland, gives back his communion token
1809  The Declaration and Address: union and freedom of conscience
1804  The Last Will: a presbytery lays down its authority for the unity of the body
1812  Brush Run: the people ordain, as kings and priests
1830  The Millennial Harbinger: a radical future, religious and social reform
Eight clicks, one breath each, in the order we told them (the Last Will, 1804, was Chapter 4, after the Declaration). Ireland: Thomas worked to reunite the Burgher and Anti-Burgher Seceders in Ulster, in the years of the 1798 rebellion and its aftermath. 1807: censured by the Presbytery of Chartiers for serving the Supper beyond the Seceders; he left them in 1808–09. Alexander in Glasgow, 1808–09: he would not take communion with a church that excluded the independents (Ewing, the Haldanes). Brush Run: Alexander ordained by the congregation, January 1812.
What they were reaching for

Five things

Unity: one body, one table
Freedom: of conscience, and of the people, over every outside authority
Laying down their own authority, so as not to stand in the way
The priesthood of all: the people take up their rightful power
A radical future: religious and social reform
Five clicks. The fifth is last week’s: the Millennial Harbinger, whose Prospectus aimed at “that political and religious order of society called THE MILLENNIUM,” with the end of sectarianism, education, and “the treatment of African slaves, as preparatory to their emancipation.”
And on every side

They were refused

1798  The Evangelical Society of Ulster: evangelism across party lines
1809  The Christian Association of Washington: a society, not a church
1810  Asks the Synod of Pittsburg for communion; refused
1811  Brush Run: a church of its own
1813  The Redstone Baptists: on their own terms, no creed
1823  The Mahoning Association, after Redstone turns against them
1830  Mahoning dissolves itself
1832  Union with Stone’s Christians
1849  The American Christian Missionary Society, by consent
Thomas Campbell helped found the Evangelical Society of Ulster in 1798, against his Synod’s objection; the Christian Association of Washington (1809) was modeled on it. Every move after reaches for the widest fellowship available, or refuses a body that makes a creed the test. Redstone: Campbell dates the “conditional union” to the fall of 1813 (MH 1848, p. 344, in Richardson); Foster gives 1815. Mahoning disbanded at Austintown in August 1830. The Stone union: Lexington, around New Year’s 1832. Campbell was president of the Missionary Society from 1849 until his death. Full timeline: database, 08 Timelines, “Campbell Associations Timeline.”
Joined, refused, dissolved · a resource

The Campbells’ associations,
1791–1866

Every church body they joined, left, were refused by, formed, or dissolved
A timeline in eight steps. Watch for two moves that keep repeating: reaching for the widest fellowship available, and refusing any body that makes a creed the test. Research: database, 08 Timelines, “Campbell Associations Timeline.”

Thomas Campbell helped found the Evangelical Society of Ulster in 1798, against his Synod’s objection; the Christian Association of Washington (1809) was modeled on it. Every move after reaches for the widest fellowship available, or refuses a body that makes a creed the test. Redstone: Campbell dates the “conditional union” to the fall of 1813 (MH 1848, p. 344, in Richardson); Foster gives 1815. Mahoning disbanded at Austintown in August 1830. Ireland

The Seceder Presbyterians

1791  Thomas licensed by the Anti-Burgher Seceder Synod of Ulster
1798  Ordained at Ahorey, Co. Armagh
1798  Helps found the Evangelical Society of Ulster, across party lines; his Synod objects
1804–05  Works to reunite Burghers and Anti-Burghers; fails
Thomas was formally an Old Light Anti-Burgher, the strictest wing, but his sympathies ran to unity and cooperation. The Evangelical Society of Ulster (1798) is the model for the Christian Association of Washington eleven years later.
Glasgow

Alexander leaves the Seceders

1808  Shipwrecked off Islay; ten months in Glasgow
1808–09  Among Greville Ewing and the Haldanes’ independents
1809  At the Seceder communion he gives back his token
The token admitted a member to the Lord’s table. Alexander returned it and did not commune: a refusal of a table fenced by a party. (Chapter 5.)
Western Pennsylvania

Out of the Presbyterians

1807  Thomas assigned to Chartiers Presbytery; charged for an open communion; walks out (Oct. 28)
1808  The Associate Synod lifts his suspension but censures him; no appointments
May 1809  Thomas withdraws from the Associate Synod
Aug. 17, 1809  The Christian Association of Washington: a society, not a church
Oct. 1810  The Synod of Pittsburg refuses it communion
September 7, 1809: Thomas reads the Declaration and Address to the Association. The Association was formed “for the sole purpose of promoting simple evangelical Christianity.” Refused by the Synod, it became a church the next spring.
A church of its own

Brush Run

May 4, 1811  Brush Run constituted; the first Supper the next day
Jan. 1, 1812  The congregation ordains Alexander
June 1812  The family immersed
Chapters 5 and 6.
Among the Baptists

Redstone and Mahoning

Fall 1813  Joins the Redstone Baptist Association on its own terms: no creed
1816  The “Sermon on the Law”
1823  The Wellsburg church; it joins the Mahoning Association
1824–26  Redstone disfellowships Brush Run and four more churches
1827  Mahoning sends out Walter Scott
Aug. 1830  Mahoning dissolves itself
Brush Run wrote out “a full view of our sentiments” and joined on condition of being left free. Campbell and Richardson date the union “the fall of 1813” (MH 1848, p. 344; Memoirs I); Foster gives 1815, perhaps the year of formal admission. Mahoning, at Austintown in August 1830, voted itself out of existence as having no scriptural standing, and met afterward only as an annual meeting for worship and reports: the Springfield Presbytery’s Last Will again.
Union

With Stone’s Christians

1827–30  Baptist associations expel the “Reformers”
1831–32  Stone, John T. Johnson and “Raccoon” John Smith prepare a union
Jan. 1832  The handshake at Lexington: a union of congregations, not organizations
Chapter 8.
Cooperation

Societies by consent

1830s–40s  District and state co-operation meetings
1843  The “Guernsey” plan: the churches of a district as one body, by consent
1845  Objects when a few men name a Bible society for the whole brotherhood
Oct. 1849  The American Christian Missionary Society: Campbell its president until his death
1861, 1863  Its war resolutions, never printed in the Harbinger
Campbell, 1845: “I doubt the propriety of any institution being got up… without a general understanding some way obtained of the concurrence and support of the whole brotherhood.” The Guernsey plan (MH Feb. 1843), Proposition 8: arrangements not enjoined in Scripture are “conventional,” “enacted by the authority of a whole community.” Walter Scott, 1844: “Who made brother Campbell an organizer over us?”
Joined, refused, dissolved

Two moves, again and again

Reach for the widest fellowship there is.
Refuse any body that makes a creed the test.
The Evangelical Society, the overture to the Synod, the Baptists, the Stone union, the cooperative societies; and Thomas leaving the Seceders, Brush Run’s terms with Redstone, Mahoning dissolving itself. Chapter 5’s “two ways not to become a sect.”

Because they would not
draw the lines where others drew them.

The Synod of Pittsburg (1810), the Baptist associations (1820s–1830), the Presbyterians (Stone, 1803). Every time: they reached for the widest fellowship, and refused any body that made a creed the test.

Can they achieve unity
with anyone?

Hold the question.
Until 1832

Our movement, our tradition

This is the movement that led to us. Until 1832, it was two.
Two movements, side by side
Stone’s Christians
Campbell’s Disciples
Known only as Christians
Known only as Disciples
No creed; “no creed but the Bible”
No creed as a test; “the Bible alone”
Unity: the Last Will dissolves their own presbytery
Unity: the Declaration and Address
An open table: they invite none, debar none
A table every Lord’s day
Each congregation governs itself
The people ordain their own elders
The end near: Christ’s kingdom breaking in
A radical future: the Millennial Harbinger
Kentucky and Ohio
Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Kentucky
Seven clicks, one row each. The same family, two names. Stone’s Christians: since the Last Will (1804), in Kentucky and Ohio; an open table (his editors’ note on Smith’s letter, 1832: “Nor debar them”); premillennial by 1832–33. Campbell’s Disciples (“Reformers” to others): put out of the Baptist associations by 1830; weekly communion; Brush Run’s ordination by the people; the Harbinger. Both: no creed as a test, the Bible alone, union. In Georgetown, in the autumn of 1831, they began to worship together.
Georgetown, autumn 1831

“We saw no reason why we should not be the same family.”

Stone and Johnson, Christian Messenger, January 1832
• “Union of Christians,” CM 6, p. 6. Stone and J. T. Johnson, in Georgetown: “the Reforming Baptists, (known invidiously, by the name of Campbellites,) and the Christians, in Georgetown and the neighborhood, agreed to meet and worship together. We soon found that we were indeed in the same spirit, on the same foundation, the New Testament, and wore the same name, Christian.”
Hill Street, Lexington
The Hill Street meetinghouse of the Christians, painted by William Clayton Bower (1955)
Saturday, December 31, 1831: a four-day meeting over New Year’s, after another at Georgetown over Christmas. Williams: “a multitude of anxious brethren began, at an early hour, to crowd the old meeting-house of the Christians, on Hill Street, in Lexington. There were Stone, and Johnson, and Smith, and Rogers, and Elley, and Creath…” (p. 450). Hill Street is now High Street; the building was demolished in the 1970s. Image: therestorationmovement.com (class use).
A mass meeting

“It was not a meeting of Elders or Preachers only, but a popular assembly…”

J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 450
• Williams goes on: “—a mass meeting of the brethren.” They came “to talk over, once more, and finally, the points of difference between them, to ascertain whether the proposed union were practicable.” Williams wrote in 1870, from Smith’s papers and memory.
“Honest doubts respecting the doctrine of the others”

What divided them

Christ: “Some Reformers still looked upon the Christians as Arians”
The Spirit: the Reformers “denied the influence of the Spirit”
Baptism: not all held “in the same sense that baptism was for the remission of sins”
The table, how open: “free or restricted communion”
The table, how often: weekly, or now and then
Clergy: who may serve the table
The name: Christian, or Disciple
Seven clicks. All from Williams, p. 450, except the last three: weekly communion (Stone: the Reformers “insisted also upon weekly communion, which we had neglected,” Biography); clergy (Stone, 1830: “the church may elect, but not ordain”; and see February 1832, below); the name (“the Christians still refused to give up their name”). The Spirit: some Christians feared the Reformers “denied the influence of the Spirit, and attached undue importance to baptism”: the Spirit’s work in conversion, not his place in the Trinity. The Trinity charge ran the other way: Christ.
Two thousand years of division
God  the Trinity · Nicaea, 325
Authority  who governs, who is clergy · 1054, 1517
The sacraments  baptism, the table · 1529
Three clicks. The same three heads as the list just shown: Christ and the Spirit; clergy; baptism and the table. They recapitulate the whole history of Christian division. (Chapter 3’s river of division, 325–1806, can be shown here: decks/elements/christendom-divisions.html.)
August Noack, Religionsgespräch zu Marburg 1529 (detail), 1867–69 · public domain
Marburg · October 1529

Luther and Zwingli.

He could not share the Lord’s table with a brother who read the Lord’s table differently.
The painting (detail): Luther, in the fur collar, holds Zwingli off; Zwingli points upward. In the full canvas Luther’s hand is on est chalked on the table (“this is my body”). Fourteen articles agreed; on the fifteenth, everything but the bodily presence. Luther: “Ihr habt einen andern Geist”, “You have a different spirit.” As the accounts have it, he would not take Zwingli’s hand as a brother’s.
→ Two men, both captive to the same Word. Only one would grant the other that.
Luther, from Marburg

“To-day the Landgrave is making every effort to unite us, or at least to make us consider each other brethren and members of Christ’s body… But although we object to be brethren, we wish to live at peace and on good terms.”

Martin Luther to Katharina, Marburg, October 4, 1529 (trans. Currie, 1908)
• Checked in the research database (Who May Ordain / Churches Refusing Each Other’s Orders, A.2; Currie, The Letters of Martin Luther, p. 197). The Lutherans’ decision, per Brenz: the Zwinglians to be acknowledged “as friends, but not as brothers and members of the church of Christ” (WA 30 III, p. 155). Luther would not take the offered hand.

Every one of these divisions
was in the room at Lexington.

All Christendom had failed to unite across them. Can two small movements in Kentucky?

The proposition

Saturday, December 31, 1831. One speaker from each side: Smith for the Disciples, Stone for the Christians.
Smith rises first

“God has but one people on the earth. He has given to them but one Book, and therein exhorts and commands them to be one family.”

“Raccoon” John Smith, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 452
• Stone had asked: “What is your choice, my brother? Will you speak first, or last?” Smith: “Brother Stone, I have no choice.” Williams: “Every eye turned upon him, and every ear leaned to catch the slightest tones of his voice.”
Not an amalgamation

“But an amalgamation of sects is not such a union as Christ prayed for, and God enjoins.”

“Raccoon” John Smith, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 452
• Checked on the page scan (the OCR scrambles “prayed for”). Next: “To agree to be one upon any system of human invention would be contrary to his will.”
One faith

“While there is but one faith, there may be ten thousand opinions; and hence, if Christians are ever to be one, they must be one in faith, and not in opinion.”

“Raccoon” John Smith, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 453
• Just before, on the Trinity and the atonement: “If I come to the passage, ‘My Father is greater than I,’ I will quote it, but will not stop to speculate upon the inferiority of the Son.” He will speak of such things “only in the words which the Lord has given.”
The proposition

“Let us, then, my brethren, be no longer Campbellites or Stoneites… but let us all come to the Bible, and to the Bible alone, as the only book in the world that can give us all the Light we need.”

“Raccoon” John Smith, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 454
• The words cut: “New Lights or Old Lights, or any other kind of lights.” He sat down.
Stone answers

“…the controversies of the Church sufficiently prove that Christians never can be one in their speculations upon those mysterious and sublime subjects…”

Barton W. Stone, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 454
• Stone: “I will not attempt to introduce any new topic.” Of his own sermons on the Trinity, forced by opposition: “I never preached a sermon of that kind that once feasted my heart; I always felt a barrenness of soul afterwards.”
His hand

“I have not one objection to the ground laid down by him as the true scriptural basis of union among the people of God; and I am willing to give him, now and here, my hand.”

Barton W. Stone, at Lexington · J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 455
• Checked on the page scan (the OCR interleaves two lines here). Williams: “He turned as he spoke, and offered to Smith a hand trembling with rapture and brotherly love, and it was grasped by a hand full of the honest pledges of fellowship.”
The handshake
Stained-glass window, Cane Ridge Meeting House (photograph: therestorationmovement.com)
Over an open Bible on the pulpit; the communion table before them, two plates and two cups. Set it against Marburg: Luther would not take the hand; Stone offered his. Maker and date of the window: unknown (to find). Class use only.
The song and the loaf

“A song arose, and brethren and sisters, with many tearful greetings, ratified and confirmed the union. On Lord’s day, they broke the loaf together…”

J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 455
• Before: “elders and teachers hastened forward, and joined their hands and hearts in joyful accord.” After: “and in that sweet and solemn communion, again pledged to each other their brotherly love.” Sunday, January 1, 1832. Williams is the only source for the communion that day; Smith’s own letter (February 1832) confirms they broke the loaf together in the weeks after.

They did not agree
on how to read it.

Uniting around the Bible was not agreeing on its interpretation: Christ, the Spirit, baptism, the table, the clergy were all still open.
The statement

“It may be asked, is there no difference of opinion among you? We answer, we do not know, nor are we concerned to know.”

Stone and Johnson, Christian Messenger, January 1832
• “Union of Christians,” CM 6, p. 6–8. Next: “We have never asked them what were their opinions, nor have they asked us. If they have opinions different from ours, they are welcome to have them, provided they do not endeavor to impose them on us as articles of faith.” And the creed: “We have a perfect one… we mean the New Testament.”
Campbell, January 2, 1832

“Is it not obvious that all lines drawn from the circumference of any circle towards its centre, will meet in the same point?”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger, January 2, 1832
“Campbellites Uniting with the Arians,” p. 36: the issue dated the day after Hill Street, written before news of it. A Georgetown man, John Brice, had written east that the “Campbellites” there had “united with the Arians” (Stone’s Christians, suspected on the Trinity). Campbell: union is not a compromise of “half their principles”; the Reformers “surrendered nothing,” and neither “Campbell nor Arius shall be the bond of union.” The loaf and cup at the centre of the drawing are ours, not his: his centre is “faith, hope, and love” (next slide).
The centre

“As all sects forsake their systems, and return to the apostolic gospel and institutions, they will meet in one and the same centre of faith, hope, and love. We devoutly wish to see Papists and Protestants, every sect coming to this centre, and then I trust they will find all those slanderously called ‘Campbellites,’ rejoicing to receive them.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger, January 2, 1832
• The same paragraph, straight on. Wide: “Papists and Protestants, every sect.” Union by everyone moving toward the centre, not toward one another’s positions.

It took three years

The differences mattered in practice. They worked them out.
Lexington, February 1832

“For they believe that no person but a preacher has a right to administer the ordinances—such as the breaking of the loaf &c. and become very much alarmed at the idea of us common folks receiving the name of kings and priests to the Lord…”

H. C. C., a Disciple in Lexington, to Campbell, Millennial Harbinger 1832, p. 192
• The two Lexington congregations pledged to “unite upon the New Testament” (Feb. 12), broke the loaf together (Feb. 19), and dissolved the pledge (Feb. 25), over choosing an elder and who may serve the table. “us common folks”: read on the page scan. His verdict: “It is the Clergy—the hireling system—the called and sent—the rulers—that keep us apart.” Side path: Who keeps the table.
Who keeps the table · a resource

Who may give thanks
for the bread?

A resource. Ask the room first: in your congregation, who gives thanks for the bread, and why that person? The answer in our churches (any disciple, not a priest) has two roots: the royal priesthood, and Matthew 18:20, where the smallest gathering is a church that may keep the Supper. It was contested from the start: in Scotland, between Campbell and Stone, and among us still. Every quote is in the document “Who keeps the table.”
Before us

“…where three are, a church is, albeit they be laics.”

Tertullian, On Exhortation to Chastity 7 (c. 210)
• The sentence before: where there is no clergy, “you offer, and baptize, and are priest, alone for yourself.” Tertullian is echoing Matthew 18:20. The old church knew the thought; it did not keep it.
Scotland

“The apparent question at issue was: may a group of believers not set in order with a presbytery eat the Lord’s Supper or not?”

D. B. Murray, on the Scotch Baptists, Baptist Quarterly (1989)
• The Scottish independents the Campbells knew in Glasgow were split on exactly this. Glasites and strict Scotch Baptists: no Supper without an elder. The Glasgow Scotch Baptists divided over “eating without elders” in 1810, the year after Alexander left. The British Churches of Christ grew from the side that ate without elders.
Two or three

“…were only two christians in any place, such as on shipboard… they ought to commemorate the death of Christ on the first day of the week…”

Ballantine’s Essays on the Elder’s Office, reprinted in Stone’s Christian Messenger (1835)
• The ground: “our Lord gives directions, Mat. xviii. 15—20. to the smallest number that might thus meet in his name.” Two or three gathered are a church, and a church keeps the Supper. (Recall Alexander on the Hibernia.)

“Is there any thing to be done at the table of the Lord, which any brother, who can give thanks for a crucified Savior, and repeat the words of the institution, cannot do?”

The same essay, in Stone’s Christian Messenger (1835)
• It goes on: to suppose “that none but an Elder can administer the Supper” attributes “some sanctity and power to an Elder which the scriptures do not warrant.” Printed in Barton Stone’s own paper.
Campbell

“‘The administration of ordinances’ is a popish phrase, and ought to be cashiered from the christian vocabulary.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian Baptist (1827)
• Answering a reader. He goes on: persons the church appoints, “when attending their respective duties,” are “administering all the ordinances.” The church’s appointment is what gives “an official right”; no sacred power passes through it.
The test of a clergy

“He would not tolerate a disciple in his church to baptize a candidate, nor to ‘administer the Lord’s supper,’ nor to pray over the loaf or the cup.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1830)
• His proof that a preacher belongs to “the aspiring priesthood”: he will not let an ordinary disciple give thanks at the table. If he does permit it, Campbell says, “I will except him from the priesthood.”
Campbell’s model church

From his memorandum book

In The Christian System, “Breaking the Loaf,” Campbell copies a Lord’s day he saw in an unnamed congregation (“The church in ——”), as “the highest approach to the model, which we have in our eye.” Not Brush Run, so far as we know; written in the 1830s. Who presided at Brush Run in 1811 is not recorded.
Who presided

“Not having any person whom they regarded as filling Paul’s outlines of a bishop, they had appointed two senior members, of a very grave deportment, to preside in their meetings. These persons were not competent to labor in the word and teaching; but they were qualified to rule well…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• About fifty members. No ordained man, and none needed: the church appointed two of its own. “One of them presided at each meeting.”
Every member a part
“He then called upon a brother… to read a section of the evangelical history.”
“…the president called upon a brother to pray in the name of the congregation.”
“…the whole congregation, brethren and sisters, pronounced aloud the final Amen.”
Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
Three clicks. The president calls on members; the members read, pray and answer. A brother also names the hymn before the table.
At the table
“…he took a small loaf from the table, and in one or two periods gave thanks for it.”
“…each one waiting upon his brother, until all were served.”
Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
Two clicks. The loaf passed “from one to another”: “no stiffness, no formality, no pageantry; all was easy, familiar, solemn, cheerful.” Campbell’s picture of the ancient order at the table.
Campbell’s verdict

“There was no stiffness, no formality, no pageantry; all was easy, familiar, solemn, cheerful.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• And: the thanksgivings were as brief “as the thanks usually presented at a common table.” Honest note: “the strangers sat off on seats more remote”; in this church the bread and cup went to the disciples.
His qualifier

“He may of right preach, baptize, and dispense the supper, as well as pray for all men, when circumstances demand it.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• Of every Christian. But: “This concession does not… authorize any individual to assume to do what has been given in charge to them” (the appointed officers). “Liberty without licentiousness, and government without tyranny.” In 1840: “Official grace and official virtue are the very essence of popery.”
Stone’s Christians

“For you cannot find in the New Testament one instance of the church having authority to ordain elders or bishops or deacons, or to administer baptism or the supper. You will find that the ministry existed before the church…”

Stone’s Christian Messenger (1830)
• Attributed to Stone by the Messenger’s index. The Christians ordained their elders, kept the Supper seldom, and held that the ordained should administer it. The exact opposite of “the fountain of official power.”
The union, 1832

“…they believe that no person but a preacher has a right to administer the ordinances — such as the breaking of the loaf…”

A letter from Lexington, Kentucky, February 1832 · Millennial Harbinger
• The month after Stone and “Raccoon” John Smith shook hands in Lexington. A local union of Christians and Reformers broke up over this: whether a church without an ordained preacher could break the loaf. They “become very much alarmed at the idea of uncommon folks receiving the name of kings and priests to the Lord.”

“When he is absent the church can do nothing. Like a widow forlorn and desolate, she is solitary and silent.”

Alexander Campbell, “The Union,” Millennial Harbinger (1832)
• Campbell’s reply, about the preacher “called and sent… to administer ordinances”: make him indispensable and the congregation cannot even meet at its own table.
The Churches of Christ settle it

“One, of course, leads in giving thanks. This is not officiating, for any disciple can do this. It does not pertain to any office.”

David Lipscomb, Queries and Answers (1910)
• Lipscomb (Gospel Advocate, Nashville): “The elders, or those who preside, can call on any disciple to do this. He only expresses aloud and leads in what every disciple does.” Our practice: members give thanks at the table; the elders arrange it.
Three paths from one table
“An ordained minister, as representative of Christ presiding at the Lord’s Table, serves in Christ’s place as host at the Table.” Disciples–Catholic dialogue, 2009
“…within Australian Churches of Christ ‘lay presidency’ is almost the norm…” Churches of Christ in Australia to the World Council, 1986
“…we have denied women the opportunity to pass Communion trays because we have described it as a ‘leadership role.’” David Kneip, Siburt Institute, ACU, 2025
Three clicks. The Disciples, in dialogue with Rome, came back to the minister as Christ’s representative; Campbell had said the one who breaks the loaf does so “not as the representative of the Lord, but after his example.” Australia kept mutual ministry. Our churches kept “any disciple” but read it as “any man,” and now argue whether passing a tray is leadership or service. In 2020 every household became its own table.

No one stands in Christ’s place.
Everyone waits on everyone.

The end of the resource. “Each one waiting upon his brother, until all were served.” Open to all; hosted by any. → Back to the spine.
Lexington, 1835

“Nor was a union between the two congregations finally and formally effected till in July, 1835…”

J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 460
• When Thomas M. Allen, preaching to the Lexington Christians, proposed it again; they “waived all prejudice and differences of opinion on the subject of order and clerical privilege” and “not only consented to the union, but nobly proposed it to the Disciples.” Williams is the only source for 1835 found so far.
Beyond Lexington

Person by person, congregation by congregation

1832  Smith (a Disciple) and Rogers (a Christian) ride together to every church
1832  Smith defends himself to his own alarmed Reformers
1834  Jacksonville, Illinois: Stone joins neither church until they unite
1835  Lexington, at last
Four clicks. Stone at Jacksonville: “I refused to unite with either until they united together, and labored to effect it. It was effected” (Biography, p. 79). Where it was slow, Stone blamed “a few ignorant, headstrong bigots on both sides.”
The union spreading, 1831–1835
Six clicks: five waves of union, then the refusals. From the database’s Gazetteer of Local Unions (36 dated unions, 15 refusals; places approximate). (1) Georgetown in the autumn of 1831, the handshake at Lexington; already, unprompted, Rush County, Indiana (“The Reforming Baptists and we, are all one here,” Dec. 1831) and Maury County, Tennessee. Stone and Johnson: “The spirit of union is spreading like fire in dry stubble.” (2) 1832: Paris, Millersburg, Carlisle (Smith’s letter), Montgomery and Bath counties, Republican (500 break the loaf), Pendleton County (“a union of all present took place”), Calloway County, McNairy County and Lock’s Creek in Tennessee. (3) Autumn 1832: the yearly meeting at Clintonville; Stone in Illinois: “a happy union of the two societies, Christians and Reformers, in one body or church” at Jacksonville; Carrollton, Jersey Prairie; Troy, Missouri. (4) 1833–34: Bowling Green and Fayette, Missouri; White River and Silver Creek, Indiana; Paris enrols as one church (Aug. 1834); Jacksonville, where Stone in 1834 found two churches again and would join neither “until they united together.” (5) July 1835: Lexington itself, at last. (6) Refused: Liberty, Indiana (1841: “we no longer seek for union with the Disciples”), Preble County, Ohio; Purviance’s Ohio churches; the eastern Christian Connection. About half of Stone’s Christians never entered the union (Encyclopedia, “Christian Connection”). Stone, 1835: “we have had no general council on this subject. Churches have acted in their private capacity.”
If asked what became of those who refused (only if it comes up): the Christian Connection merged with the Congregationalists (1931), then into the United Church of Christ (1957). The Disciples and the UCC: “Declaration of Ecumenical Partnership” (1985), “full communion” (1989), after the Disciples recognized infant baptism as “a legitimate form of baptism” (1987). Recognition, not agreement. The UCC receives the creeds “as testimonies, but not tests of the faith.” (Encyclopedia; ucc.org.)

No magic moment.
It was worked out.

Visible unity came over years, with patience and forbearance, exploring together. Smith called it “the best act of his life” (Williams, p. 456); Stone, “the noblest act of my life” (Biography, p. 79).

And it worked:
one movement, one history.

We look back on it as shared history. Today it is one movement, in three streams.
For discussion

Are we more Stone,
or more Campbell?

For discussion. Weekly communion (Campbell); the open table (Stone); baptism for remission (Campbell); elders and preachers; the name; revival and the Spirit (Stone). It gets confusing, and that is the point.
The quiz, again

No creed but…

…Christ.
…the Bible.
Two clicks: the room’s two answers. “No creed but the Bible” is Stone’s own phrase (1828, 1832); “No creed but Christ” grows out of Walter Scott’s creed and is a slogan by the 1900s. Side path: No creed but….
Two proposals?

“…to state the anomaly as boldly as possible, the movement is at one and the same time Christocentric and bibliocentric.”

Dwight E. Stevenson, Disciples Panel of Scholars (1963)
• As quoted in the Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement, “Faith.” Paul Blowers summarizes him: the two slogans are “very different proposals, as different as allegiance to Christ and allegiance to the strict letter of the scriptural text.”
Scott, the year of Lexington

“…her only manual was, ‘The Bible.’ And her all comprehensive creed for the binding of the faithful; ‘Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’”

Walter Scott, The Evangelist (1832), “Primitive Sufferings,” p. 32
• Of the first church. “On this faith and this volume she gathered her children thick as the leaves in Autumn.” The Bible the manual; Christ the creed. Both of the room’s answers, in one sentence. Side path follows.
No creed but… · a resource

No creed but…

The quiz, answered. The room will have said “Christ” and “the Bible.” Both have a history: the first is Stone’s own phrase; the second grows out of Walter Scott’s creed, and became a slogan later. For Scott in 1832 they were one thing. Every quote is in the document “No creed but…”.
Stone

“We determined that we would own no name but Christian… and that we would subscribe to no creed but the Bible…”

Barton W. Stone, Christian Messenger (1828)
• “Reply to Elder John Powell’s Queries, No. III,” p. 231. The name: “which we derive from our union with Christ.” It goes on: “if we were deprived of the fellowship of any Christians, it should be by an act of theirs and not of ours.”
Stone, to a Presbyterian

“You know, sir, that I owned no creed but the Bible, and that I was ordained with this understanding by the Presbytery.”

Barton W. Stone, letter to J. L. Wilson, Christian Messenger (1832)
• Wilson was the Presbyterian minister in Cincinnati who had written against the New Lights. Stone’s ordination at Cane Ridge (1798): he accepted the Westminster Confession only “as far as I see it consistent with the word of God.”
At Lexington

“After we had given up all creeds and taken the Bible, and the Bible alone, as our rule of faith and practice…”

Stone at Lexington, Dec. 31, 1831, in Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870)
• p. 454. Stone answering Smith, just before the handshake. Williams wrote in 1870; the words are his reconstruction.
Walter Scott

“Behold my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.” … he proposes it for the religious creed of all the world…

Walter Scott, The Evangelist (1832)
• p. 3, the opening of Scott’s paper, the year of Lexington. “He” is the Father, speaking at the Jordan. Scott calls it “this illustrious Oracle”; the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, is the creed.
The first church

“…her only manual was, ‘The Bible.’ And her all comprehensive creed for the binding of the faithful; ‘Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’”

Walter Scott, The Evangelist (1832), “Primitive Sufferings”
• p. 32. It goes on: “On this faith and this volume she gathered her children thick as the leaves in Autumn.” The Bible is the manual; Christ is the creed. Both answers to the quiz, in one sentence, in 1832.
Scott, 1832
Her manual: the Bible.
Her creed: Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
Two clicks. Not rival answers: one is the book, the other is the confession. “On this faith and this volume.”
Scott, 1859

“It shows the true creed, and restores it to its native eminence above all other things in the gospel.”

Walter Scott, The Messiahship (1859)
• p. 272, of the Messiahship, the confession that Jesus is the Christ. p. 211: “the creed, built exclusively on Christ as the Son of the living God.” p. 273: “As a creed, it is exclusive of all foreign matter, and will make no concession to, or compromises with any other creed, Catholic or Protestant.”
Scott, 1859

“By a series of negations, I might exclude every creed in Christendom from its claims to be called the creed of our religion…”

Walter Scott, The Messiahship (1859)
• pp. 274–275 (page to confirm). And arrive, he says, at the Messiahship. A creed of one article, a person.
What was ours

“…if any section of the Christian profession offers it in its practical forms as the basis of Christian union, the symbol of confession for the remission of sins, and the element of our perfection in holiness, save our brethren, the author is not aware of it.”

Walter Scott, The Messiahship (1859), preface
• p. 7. “It” is “the great oracle that ‘Jesus is the Christ.’” Scott does not claim to have restored it; he claims his brethren alone made it the basis of union. Note: the phrase “golden oracle” is not in Scott’s texts in our database; it is the title of Dwight Stevenson’s biography of him (1946).
The slogan

“We have no authority but the Bible; we wear no name but ‘Christians;’ and we have no creed but Christ.”

T. W. Phillips, chairman, Centennial Convention, Pittsburgh (1909)
• The centennial of the Declaration and Address. By then the full slogan ran: “No creed but Christ, no book but the Bible, no law but love, no name but the divine” (Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement, “Slogans”; no known author). The earliest uses in our corpus are 1909 and Garrison (1926).
The two answers

“…to state the anomaly as boldly as possible, the movement is at one and the same time Christocentric and bibliocentric.”

Dwight E. Stevenson, Disciples Panel of Scholars (1963)
• “Faith versus Theology in the Thought of the Disciple Fathers,” The Renewal of Church, vol. 2, pp. 33–60, as quoted in the Encyclopedia (“Faith”). Stevenson taught preaching at the College of the Bible (Lexington Theological Seminary) and wrote Walter Scott: Voice of the Golden Oracle. Paul Blowers’s summary of him: the two slogans are “very different proposals, as different as allegiance to Christ and allegiance to the strict letter of the scriptural text.” Scott held them together; later readers pulled them apart.

Different proposals,
only if we forget what they meant.

Micah, in his own voice: he prefers “No creed but Christ.” Uniting on the Bible was never uniting on opinions about the Bible. Smith, the same morning: “no deduction or inference from them, however logical or true, forms any part of the Gospel of Jesus Christ” (Williams, p. 453).
Their only Leader

“The brethren of Stone did not join Alexander Campbell as their leader, nor did the brethren of Campbell join Barton W. Stone as their leader; but each, having already taken Jesus the Christ as their only Leader, in love and liberty became one body…”

J. A. Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (1870), p. 456
• Williams’s summary of what the handshake meant (1870). It goes on: “not Stoneites, or Campbellites; not Christians, or Disciples, distinctively as such; but Christians, Disciples, saints, brethren, and children of the same Father.” Before it: “an equal and mutual pledge and resolution to meet on the Bible as on common ground, and to preach the Gospel rather than to propagate opinions.”

A shared practice:
coming to Scripture to meet Christ.

What that looked like, person by person and congregation by congregation, could be as far apart as all the historic streams of Christianity. And still they held that it could bring them together.
Idea 1 of 4

They united around the Bible,
not their readings of it.

Smith: “one in faith, and not in opinion.” Stone and Johnson: “we do not know, nor are we concerned to know.”
Idea 2 of 4

Every historic division
came to one table.

God, authority, the sacraments: what had divided Christendom since Nicaea was in the room at Hill Street.
Idea 3 of 4

Unity was not a moment.
It was worked out.

Three years in Lexington; person by person, congregation by congregation elsewhere.
Idea 4 of 4

No creed but Christ;
the Bible as our manual.

Scott, 1832: the Bible “her only manual,” “Jesus Christ is the Son of God” her creed. Williams: each had “already taken Jesus the Christ as their only Leader.”
Today’s ideas
1.They united around the Bible, not their readings of it.
2.Every historic division came to one table.
3.Unity was not a moment. It was worked out.
4.No creed but Christ; the Bible as our manual.
All four at once, before the discussion.

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?
